Wind turbine power curve modeling using radial basis function neural
networks and tabu search

abstract
Wind turbine power curve (WTPC) modeling is of great importance for performance monitoring. This
work proposes a new method for producing highly accurate non-parametric models for wind turbines
based on arti ﬁcial neural networks (ANNs). To achieve this, we employ networks belonging to the radial
basis function (RBF) architecture, and feed them with additional important input variables besides wind
speed. To further increase modeling accuracy, while at the same time keeping the computational cost at
acceptable levels, we introduce a new training algorithm based on the successful non-symmetric fuzzy
means (NSFM) approach, which in this work is hybridized with the tabu search (TS) metaheuristic
technique, enabling the method to train ef ﬁciently datasets of high dimensionality. The resulting method
is evaluated on real data from four wind turbines, whereas a comparison with numerous WTPC modeling
schemes, including parametric and non-parametric models is conducted. The solution found by the
proposed algorithm outperforms the results produced by its rivals in terms of both modeling accuracy
and ef ﬁciency, while in most cases it also leads to simpler models. The resulting models can be used
successfully, not only for accurate WTPC modeling, but also for constructing wind turbine performance
analysis tools, e.g. 3-D power curves.

1. Introduction
Energy is essential for economic and social development; on the
other hand, it poses an environmental challenge as the global
population grows and therefore all aspects of energy production
and consumption should be addressed [ 1]. The urgent need to
reduce the pollutant emissions that come as byproducts of energy
production and the ﬁniteness of the earth ’s fossil fuel reserves,
make renewable energy to be part of the solution for the energy
problem [2]. Since antiquity, mankind has been using wind power,
but its reappearance as an important source of energy began at the
end of the 20th century as a notable development; indeed, nowa-
days, wind energy appears to be one of the cost-effective options
for electricity generation [ 1,2].
The theoretical power output ( P) from a modern wind turbine

The electrical power output of a wind turbine as a function of
the wind speed is shown in a graph, known as the power curve [ 2].
Given a typical wind turbine, the power curve (WTPC) consists of
three key wind speed points: (i) the cut-in speed, i.e. the minimum
speed of wind so that the turbine is able to generate power, (ii) the
rated wind speed, i.e. the wind speed necessary for reaching the
rated power and (iii) the cut-out speed, i.e. the maximum wind
speed for which the wind turbine is allowed to generate power. At
high values of wind speed, the produced power is limited by en-
gineering design, while there are three strategies that are used to
control the speed of the wind to prevent from damaging the wind
turbine: pitch, yaw and stall control [ 2]. Modern wind turbines are
pitch-controlled, i.e. power output is kept constant at wind speeds
above the rated value [ 4].

atmospheric pressure, turbulence intensity and wind direction
variability, among others [ 5].
Wind turbine power curve modeling is an essential tool in tur-
bine performance monitoring and power prediction or forecasting
[6], and therefore developing accurate models for WTPC is
considered as a very important area of research [ 7]. Moreover, the
power curve of a wind turbine helps in obtaining a rough wind
energy estimation without taking into account technical details of
its generating system [2]. There are several statistical techniques to
ﬁt the power curve of a wind turbine to data from real-world
operation, which can be classi ﬁed into parametric and non-
parametric methods [ 6e8]. To de ﬁne the relationship between
input variables and output response in a parametric model, a set of
mathematical equations consisting of a ﬁnite number of parame-
ters is assumed. Though parametric equations may contain free
parameters that can be ﬁtted to actual data, they have a ﬁxed form,
which is based on the underlying physical laws. A non-parametric
approach, on the other hand, makes no a priori assumptions
regarding the form of the governing equations, which in this case is
determined by the available data [ 9]. Notwithstanding their name,
non-parametric models also make use of parameters, but, in
contrast to parametric models, the number and nature of these
parameters are ﬂexible and not ﬁxed in advance [ 7].
Although the shape of the wind turbine power curve has, in
some cases, encouraged the choice of parametric models, their
application is associated with certain limitations [ 6], as they are
usually complex to use, while they are considered to be less accu-
rate in describing the actual behavior of real-world wind turbines
[10]. Non-parametric models, on the other hand, appear to be more
ﬂexible, and thus more precise, in terms of accurately modeling
power curves [ 6], their main drawback being the increased
computational cost compared to parametric ones. In what follows,
a review of recent literature is presented, while a comprehensive
list of WTPC modeling techniques can be found in Ref. [ 9].
In Ref. [ 6], WTPC is modelled using advanced parametric and
non-parametric methods. The results of this study suggest that
penalized spline regression presents a better performance over
other analyzed methods. In Ref. [ 11], parametric models are
developed for WTPC, based on non-linear regression functions. The
models take into account the wind speed, while the wind direction
impact on power curve is tested. Wind farm power curve models
have also been published in literature; e.g. in Ref. [ 12], wind farm
performance monitoring is accomplished by using three different
operational curves.
More elaborate non-parametric methods have been applied to
wind turbine systems (e.g. predicting the generated wind power in
wind farms), involving computational intelligence (CI) techniques
[13], which can be more ef ﬁcient and accurate than traditional
statistical methods [ 14]. CI consists of nature-inspired computa-
tional tools, such as evolutionary computation, swarm intelligence,
fuzzy logic and arti ﬁcial neural networks (ANNs), which have been
used extensively to solve a wide range of complex problems. ANNs
constitute an important tool in the ﬁeld of CI that tries to simulate
some properties of biological neural networks as found in the hu-
man brain, through a “black-box” approach; ANNs can model an
unknown system without any prior knowledge for its behavior,
based solely on input and output data [ 15]. In the next paragraph,
works of literature dealing with CI models for WTPC are discussed
brieﬂy, whereas a survey of ANNs in wind energy systems is given
in Ref. [ 16].
In Ref. [7], a differential evolution algorithm has been employed
for the estimation of a ﬁve-parameter logistic function for WTPC
modeling. Non-parametric models have been developed as well,
including ANN, fuzzy c-means clustering and data mining tech-
niques using the wind speed as input variable. The results are
favorable for the parametric model, while the ANN is claimed to be
the best nonparametric model. In Ref. [ 17], parametric and non-
parametric methods, including multi-layer perceptron (MLP) net-
works and genetic algorithms, are used to build models for power
prediction that can be used for on-line monitoring of wind farms.
The k-nearest neighbor model results in a good performance for the
wind farm operating in normal conditions. In Ref. [ 18], different
non-parametric methods based on various neural network archi-
tectures are constructed for WTPC modeling; the produced models
can also be used to estimate the reference power curve for on-line
monitoring of wind farm performance. In Ref. [ 19], non-parametric
models, including ANNs, are developed for power curve moni-
toring; it is shown that when the ambient temperature and wind
direction are considered as input parameters along with wind
speed, the prediction errors are reduced, while the model is capable

three kernel functions is used to build power curve models, which
are compared with models published in literature; results show
that there exists a data partition which can lead to satisfactory
performance. In Ref. [ 22], an ANN with two inputs is constructed,
and, combined with gaussian process ﬁltering, it leads to an accu-
rate method for calculating wind direction-dependent power
curves. In Ref. [ 23], a comparison of modeling methods for wind
power prediction is conducted, where various parametric and non-
parametric models, including ANNs are developed for power curve
modeling. The study of the effect of input parameters in wind po-
wer prediction is the main contribution of this work. The prediction
results are favorable for the ANNs, as they come with the lowest
values of metric errors, due to their inherent universal approxi-
mation characteristic. In Ref. [ 24], an MLP network with several
inputs is trained and optimized using a genetic algorithm to model
WTPC; the proposed ANN model achieves a satisfactory perfor-
mance when compared to Fourier series interpolation, as it takes
into account simultaneously up to ten important climatic variables
that inﬂuence power output.
The contribution of the above recently-published works is
essential, as the estimations of neural network models produced by
well-known and tested training algorithms are improved in
conjunction with either speci ﬁc ﬁltering procedures, or parameter
optimization techniques. However, the latter usually increase
considerably the computational cost, which is already high due to
the data-driven nature of non-parametric approaches, thus
impeding their use in large-volume datasets; moreover, further
improvement in terms of modeling accuracy and/or computational
efﬁciency could be achieved by employing novel, non-standard
training algorithms, or even different ANN architectures
compared to standard MLPs.
Radial basis function (RBF) networks are a special type of feed-
forward neural networks that consist of a single hidden layer [ 25].
Their simple structure provides several important advantages
regarding speed and efﬁciency when compared to different popular
architectures, like MLPs, while they are also characterized by the
universal approximation property, robustness, good generalization
and very competitive results compared to other machine learning
approaches [26]. RBF neural networks have been successfully applied
to wind energy systems [16]; for example, in Ref. [27], three different
ANN architectures, including RBFNs, are employed for short term
wind speed forecasting. In Ref. [28], an improved RBF neural network
with an error feedback scheme is developed for short-term wind
speed forecasting, proposing a parameter initialization and intro-
ducing a shape parameter in the Gaussian basis function.
Surprisingly, despite the signi ﬁcant advantages offered by the
RBF architecture, only a small number of published works employ
them for wind power estimation. In Ref. [ 29], an RBF neural
network is trained for wind power prediction and appears to be
superior to MLP networks. Earlier attempts concern classic training
algorithms, as for example in Ref. [ 4], where fuzzy modeling
techniques and ANNs are used to estimate the annual energy
output of a wind turbine. The RBF network in this study comes with
a pre-ﬁxed hidden layer size and makes use of Gaussian kernels. In
a recent work [ 30], an RBF neural network is developed for wind
power prediction, using a hybrid particle swarm optimization
(PSO)-based fuzzy c-means clustering procedure and extreme
learning machines.
In this paper, the beneﬁts of the RBF architecture are exploited in
order to build a new non-parametric method for modeling the
power curve of wind turbines with increased accuracy. The method
allows to take into account large amounts of data and multiple
inputs that affect power generation besides wind speed. The
network parameters are determined automatically through a novel
training procedure based on the non-symmetric fuzzy partitioning
(NSFM) algorithm of the input space [31
]. Variants of this algorithm
have been shown to offer increased accuracy in different applica-
tions, but require tedious search procedures for parameter opti-
mization, which involve either exhaustive search [ 32], or
population-based metaheuristic search methods [ 31,33]; such ap-
proaches impose a high computational burden and coupling them
with a non-parametric training procedure - which is by itself
computationally demanding - may render the scheme impractical
for use on large datasets. An important contribution of this work,
concerns the introduction of a modi ﬁed tabu search (TS) meta-
heuristic technique [ 34], which is wrapped around the NSFM al-
gorithm; the proposed approach is not population-based, but
rather acts on a single solution, thus helping to obtain the network
parameters at an acceptable computational cost, even when using
high-volume datasets, and ultimately rendering the method suit-
able for producing highly accurate models for WTPC modeling.
The outline of this paper is as follows: in section 2 a description
of the available data is given; section 3 presents an introduction to
artiﬁcial neural networks, which is followed by a description of the
RBF network architecture and the fuzzy means training algorithm;
in section 4 standard tabu search is presented followed by a
detailed description of the proposed method; in section 5 the case
study is described and the results are presented, whereas section 6
summarizes the conclusions of the current study, and provides
plans for future work.
2. Data description
The proposed approach for power curve modeling was evalu-
ated on data from four different pitch-controlled wind turbines
belonging to the same wind farm. The location of the wind farm is
not disclosed due to con ﬁdentiality reasons. The collected data
correspond to a time period of 1 year and were recorded in 10-min
intervals, amounting to a total of approximately 50k datapoints for
each wind turbine. Wind data are measured by nacelle
anemometers.
Scatter power curves based on the raw data for the four wind
turbines are depicted in Fig. 1. As it can be seen, the plots deviate
from the typical form of the power curve obtained in standard
conditions by manufacturers. This is expected, as typically power
curves contain abnormal values that are characterized as outliers:
wind speed values close to the cut-in or the cut-out speed, negative
power values, non-operational periods, invalid, missing or cor-
rupted data due to sensor and pitch malfunction, dirt or icing on
blades, etc. [ 35]. To this end, a ﬁltering process is used to ﬁlter out
erroneous data in order to eliminate the impact of different oper-
ating conditions. More details about the ﬁltering procedure fol-
lowed in this work can be found in section 5.1.
As soon as datasets are ﬁltered out and cleared from outliers, a
model for power curve approximation can be developed based on
qualitative data. In order to increase estimation accuracy, the data-
driven models produced in this work make use of four additional
input variables besides wind speed, which have been shown in the
literature to have a strong in ﬂuence on the generated power,
namely the wind direction and ambient temperature [ 19], and the
blade pitch angle [ 23,36].
More precisely, wind direction ﬂuctuations, and hence turbu-
lence intensity variations due to ﬁeld conditions such as

3. Arti ﬁcial neural networks
3.1. Introduction
Artiﬁcial neural networks constitute one of the most important
computational intelligence tools and are used in a wide variety of
problems, including function approximation and pattern recogni-
tion [ 25]. As their name implies, ANNs are inspired by biological
neural networks; leaving aside complicated biological terms, each
neuron in a biological neural network receives an input and
transmits an output signal to all the connected neurons, according
to the amount of its activation. Correspondingly, an ANN consists of
many computational units which try to imitate this operation,
called arti ﬁcial neurons, or more simply, neurons. Each neuron
receives an input and produces an output which depends on the
value of a mathematical function, usually known as the activation
function.
ANNs are characterized by many special properties [ 13];
perhaps the most important of them is learning through examples,
a process called training. In short, during the training stage the ANN
parameters are estimated, so that a speci ﬁc input yields the

3.2. Radial basis function networks
Radial basis function networks (RBFNs) constitute an important
ANN architecture, proposed independently by Broomhead, Lowe
and other researchers at the end of the 80 ’s[ 37]. The typical
structure of RBF networks used in this work is illustrated in Fig. 2.
RBFNs are feed-forward networks with one input layer, one hidden
layer and one output layer. The input layer distributes the
normalized input variables to the L hidden units of the hidden layer.
Each hidden unit implements a radial basis function (hence the
name of the network), associated to a center vector, with dimen-
sionality equal to the number of input variables. The latter leads to a
non-linear connection between the input and the hidden layer,
while the output layer is linearly attached to the hidden layer [ 31].
Due to their simple structure, RBF networks present important
advantages regarding speed and ef ﬁciency when compared to
other popular architectures like MLP networks [ 31,38].

3.3. Symmetric and non-symmetric fuzzy means algorithm
Contrary to the k-means algorithm, where clustering is con-
ducted discretely and every datapoint belongs explicitly to one
speciﬁc cluster, following the fuzzy logic approach [ 44] the data-
points may belong to more than one fuzzy set, according to a
membership degree. To materialize the fuzzy means algorithm,
therefore, which performs fuzzy partitioning of an N-D dimensional
input space, a total of K datapoints are considered. Initially, the
domain of each variable is partitioned into a number
si ði ¼ 1; 2; …; NÞ of triangular one-dimensional fuzzy sets. The
combinations of fuzzy sets from each dimension produce the so-
called fuzzy subspaces; the input space is partitioned into a total
of S fuzzy subspaces, which is equal to the product of the number of
fuzzy sets in each dimension. The algorithm then seeks a subset
consisting of L fuzzy subspaces which are chosen so that they
uniformly cover the distribution of the input space and whose
centers will constitute the RBF network centers. This is accom-
plished through a non-iterative procedure, which leads to a fast RBF
center selection process, even in the case of big datasets [ 26].
If the number of fuzzy sets is the same for every dimension ðs1 ¼
s2 ¼ … ¼ sN Þ, the partitioning is considered to be symmetric,
which leads to the standard symmetric fuzzy means (SFM) algo-
rithm. In this case, the only parameter to be chosen by the user is
the number of fuzzy sets, which is common for all dimensions. This
number affects the size of the network and thus, its estimation and
generalization capabilities.
On the other hand, a non-symmetric partitioning (where sis sj;
isj), could lead to RBF networks presenting greater ﬂexibility, with
the potential to achieve better estimation accuracy [ 31]. Imple-
menting this non-symmetric partitioning leads to the non-
symmetric fuzzy means (NSFM) algorithm, which is based on the
same basic principles with standard SFM, with the difference that
this time the user has to select N different parameters, i.e. the
vector comprising the numbers of fuzzy sets, which are now
different for each dimension.
For systems consisting of a low number of input variables N, this
selection could be performed using a trial and error procedure
where all the combinations of fuzzy sets per dimension are tested.
However, in systems with large, or even moderate dimensionalities,
an exhaustive search for all possible combinations may lead to very
high computational times, making the use of NSFM algorithm
impractical. Therefore, more efﬁcient ways have to be incorporated,
in order to ﬁnd an adequate fuzzy partitioning of the input space
with respect to network performance in a reasonable time.
In such cases where exact methods are too expensive to apply,
one has to utilize more ef ﬁcient ways in order to obtain suf ﬁciently
good, but possible not globally optimal, solutions. Within this
context, the NSFM algorithm was successfully coupled with meta-
heuristic search methods belonging to evolutionary computation
[33] and swarm intelligence [ 31]. Such techniques are based on a
population of potential solutions, which are evolved over a number
of iterations. Although these approaches can yield signi ﬁcant
beneﬁts when compared to the impractical exhaustive search
procedure, they are still considered to be computationally expen-
sive due to the need to maintain a population of potential solutions,
which leads to a signi ﬁcant number of function evaluations per
each iteration. The problem becomes more apparent for systems
with a large number of datapoints and/or input variables.
As the datasets involved in this work, which have been
described in section 2, fall into this category, we introduce a new,
less computationally demanding method for implementing the
NSFM algorithm in order to produce accurate RBF networks for
WTPC modeling. This is achieved by coupling the NSFM algorithm
with a metaheuristic search method known as tabu search (TS)
[34], which, in contrast to the aforementioned population-based
methods, evolves only a single solution, and thus is more appro-
priate for large datasets.
4. Tabu search e non symmetric fuzzy means (TS-NSFM)
algorithm
4.1. Standard tabu search
Along with different approaches that ﬁnd application in the
context of metaheuristic methods, such as genetic algorithms and
particle swarm optimization, TS has also been designed to avoid
being trapped in local optima by using heuristics to explore the so-
lution space beyond local optimality. Its popularity has signi ﬁcantly
grown during the last decades, as it is characterized as the most
efﬁcient method for handling large scale optimization problems [45].
TS can be thought as an iterative descent method, starting with a
randomly generated initial solution and examining the neighbor-
hood around it. However, in contrast to classical descent methods,
for example the steepest descent method, where the algorithm
terminates as soon as the solution stops improving, in the TS al-
gorithm there is no such a restriction: non-improving solutions can
be accepted, in order to avoid being trapped in local minima.
Therefore, in the latter, the process continues from the best solution
found in the current neighborhood, while the best solution found
so far is stored. It must be noted, however, that in order to avoid
revisiting previously visited solutions, the algorithm makes use of a
list, known as tabu list (TL). The TL contains the history of the search
and is characterized as the most distinctive feature of tabu search
[46]. This list has a ﬁxed size |TL| and is updated by adding the last
moves to the beginning of the list and discarding the oldest ele-
ments, if necessary. All the moves back to solutions being stored in
the TL are called tabu moves and are forbidden for the next |TL|
iterations. The size of the TL affects the search process in the sense
that increased sizes result in a more likely rejection of a new so-
lution, leading the search in areas which have not recently been
tested. Tabu status can be recalled, provided that a condition
known as aspiration criterion (AC), is satis ﬁed. The AC allows the
algorithm to perform moves even if they have been characterized
as tabu. For example, a tabu move can lose its tabu status under the
condition that it yields a solution with better objective function
value than the best found so far; this condition is known as aspi-
ration by objective.
The above description concerns the standard TS procedure, over
which many improvements have been introduced in the literature
[47]. These modi ﬁcations may include multiple aspiration criteria
and tabu lists, variable tabu list sizes, systematic intensi ﬁcation and
diversiﬁcation strategies for neighborhood creation, long term
memory implementation and many others, depending on the in-
dividual problem at hand. In this work, the basic TS algorithm is
adapted so as to facilitate the search for a fuzzy partitioning which
results to models with increased accuracy.

6. Conclusions
This paper introduces a new method for producing highly ac-
curate power curve models of wind turbines, by taking into account
other important variables besides wind speed, namely the wind
direction, ambient temperature and blade pitch angle in this case.
The method concerns the development of a non-parametric model
and, in particular, an RBF neural network, which is characterized by

its simple architecture. The network parameters are determined

which presents greater ﬂexibility in parameter selection compared
to the standard symmetric version, thus producing networks of
increased accuracy. As the increased number of inputs and the
signiﬁcant amount of data which are needed for training a model of
high accuracy render the use of exhaustive search, or even
population-based metaheuristic search methods impractical, we
propose a novel approach based on a modi ﬁcation of the TS met-
aheuristic technique, which results to the TS-NSFM algorithm. To
evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm, a set of ex-
periments was conducted using four wind turbine datasets and, in
order to further demonstrate the ef ﬁciency of the modeling
approach, a number of parametric and non-parametric modeling
methods, including three different MLP network-based schemes,
were included for comparison. The comparative results are in favor
of the TS-NSFM algorithm, as it achieves to produce models with
higher accuracy compared to all its rivals, while also outperforming
the other ANN approaches in terms of shorter computational times.
Moreover, the proposed models can be applied for building wind
turbine performance analysis tools, as con ﬁrmed by the produced
graphs in both 2-D and 3-D cases, constructed based on the model
estimations.
Future research plans include applying the proposed algorithm
to address other challenging applications in wind energy systems,
such as forecasting, or fault detection and diagnostics; taking
advantage of the remarkable features of RBFN, it is expected that
ﬂexible models with increased accuracy can be developed in
shorter computational times.
